units.title: Concurrency vs Parallelism
units.tip: Concurrency is about managing multiple tasks that can start, run, and finish in overlapping periods. Parallelism is running tasks simultaneously on multiple processors. A single-core CPU can do concurrency but not parallelism.

exercises.question: What is concurrency?
exercises.answer: Multiple tasks making progress during overlapping time periods
exercises.explain: Concurrency means tasks are interleaved and can start before others finish. A single core can achieve concurrency by switching between tasks.
choices: Multiple tasks making progress during overlapping time periods
Only working on one thing at a time
Multiple tasks running at the exact same time on different cores
Tasks waiting for each other to complete

exercises.question: Can a single-core processor achieve concurrency?
exercises.answer: Yes, by switching between tasks quickly
exercises.explain: A single core can switch between tasks so fast it appears concurrent. The operating system uses a scheduler to allocate CPU time to different tasks.
choices: Only if tasks never block
No, concurrency requires multiple cores
Only if tasks are running on different machines
Yes, by switching between tasks quickly

exercises.question: What is the primary advantage of concurrent programming?
exercises.answer: Tasks can make progress while others wait for I/O
exercises.explain: When one task blocks on I/O (disk, network, user input), the scheduler switches to another task. This keeps the processor busy instead of idle.
choices: It always makes programs faster
It guarantees tasks complete in order
Tasks can make progress while others wait for I/O
It eliminates the need for operating systems

exercises.question: In a web server handling client requests, why is concurrency useful?
exercises.answer: While one client waits for database results, the server handles other clients
exercises.explain: Concurrency allows a server to accept a new request while another is blocked waiting for data. This improves throughput and responsiveness.
choices: It reduces memory usage
It eliminates security issues
While one client waits for database results, the server handles other clients
It makes each individual request faster

exercises.question: What is an example of concurrency in a smartphone?
exercises.answer: Playing music while browsing the web and downloading a file
exercises.explain: Even on a phone with a few cores, the OS schedules many tasks: music playback, network downloads, UI rendering, and background services. They interleave to appear simultaneous.
choices: Completing all tasks in strict order
Running tasks only when the user is active
Opening one app at a time
Playing music while browsing the web and downloading a file

exercises.question: What is parallelism?
exercises.answer: Multiple tasks running simultaneously on different processors
exercises.explain: Parallelism requires multiple cores or processors. Tasks run at the same wall-clock time, not just interleaved.
choices: Multiple tasks running simultaneously on different processors
Multiple tasks interleaved on one core
Tasks communicating with each other
Tasks running in sequence one after another

exercises.question: Can you have concurrency without parallelism?
exercises.answer: Yes, on a single-core processor
exercises.explain: Concurrency is a software concept about overlapping task periods. Parallelism is a hardware capability. Concurrency works on single-core via task switching.
choices: Yes, on a single-core processor
Only on modern multi-core systems
Only if tasks don't use the CPU
No, they are the same thing

exercises.question: Which statement correctly contrasts concurrency and parallelism?
exercises.answer: Concurrency is about structuring tasks to overlap in time; parallelism is about executing them at the same instant
exercises.explain: Concurrency describes how a program is organized so tasks can overlap. Parallelism describes tasks literally running at the same moment on separate processors.
choices: Concurrency only exists on multi-core machines
They are exactly the same thing
Parallelism is about structuring tasks; concurrency requires multiple processors
Concurrency is about structuring tasks to overlap in time; parallelism is about executing them at the same instant

exercises.question: A dual-core CPU running two tasks: which term applies?
exercises.answer: Both concurrency and parallelism
exercises.explain: Parallelism describes the hardware execution (two cores, simultaneous). Concurrency describes the program design (two independent tasks). Both terms are correct.
choices: Neither, they are sequential
Only parallelism
Both concurrency and parallelism
Only concurrency

exercises.question: Why is concurrent design important even on single-core systems?
exercises.answer: It allows responsive programs that don't block the user interface
exercises.explain: Concurrency prevents long tasks from freezing the UI. Even on one core, concurrent design lets background work happen while the UI remains responsive.
choices: It makes the program run faster
It allows responsive programs that don't block the user interface
It is only useful on multi-core systems
It eliminates all blocking operations

units.title: Threads and Processes
units.tip: A process is an independent program with its own memory and resources. A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process that shares memory with other threads. Threads are cheaper to create and switch between than processes.

exercises.question: What is a process?
exercises.answer: An independent program instance with its own memory and resources
exercises.explain: A process is an isolated execution environment. Each process has its own heap, stack, file descriptors, and system resources. The OS protects processes from interfering with each other.
choices: A single task within a program
An independent program instance with its own memory and resources
A request from the user
A function call

exercises.question: Why is memory isolation important between processes?
exercises.answer: One process crash does not take down others; malicious code cannot easily access other programs
exercises.explain: Process isolation protects stability and security. If one process crashes, it does not corrupt memory belonging to other processes. A bug in one program cannot directly read another's data.
choices: It makes programs run faster
One process crash does not take down others; malicious code cannot easily access other programs
It eliminates the need for synchronization
It reduces the number of cores needed

exercises.question: How do two processes communicate?
exercises.answer: Through operating system mechanisms: pipes, sockets, message queues, shared files
exercises.explain: Processes cannot directly read each other's memory. They must use OS-provided IPC (inter-process communication) mechanisms to exchange data.
choices: They cannot communicate
Through operating system mechanisms: pipes, sockets, message queues, shared files
Only through the file system
By reading each other's memory directly

exercises.question: What is the cost of creating a new process?
exercises.answer: High; each process needs its own memory space and OS resources
exercises.explain: Creating a process is expensive. The OS must allocate memory, set up a page table, initialize file descriptors, and other overhead. This is much heavier than creating a thread.
choices: High; each process needs its own memory space and OS resources
Nearly free
Negligible compared to computation
The same as creating a thread

exercises.question: In a multitasking OS, what happens when a process blocks on I/O?
exercises.answer: The OS scheduler switches to another process; the blocked process is suspended
exercises.explain: When a process blocks (waits for network, disk, or user input), the scheduler pauses it and runs another process. The blocked process resumes once its I/O completes.
choices: The OS scheduler switches to another process; the blocked process is suspended
The process spins in a loop checking for I/O completion
The blocked process gets more CPU time to compensate
All processes freeze until the I/O completes

exercises.question: What is a thread?
exercises.answer: A lightweight unit of execution within a process that shares memory with other threads
exercises.explain: A thread is a path of execution within a process. Multiple threads in one process share the same heap and global variables but each has its own stack.
choices: A function in a program
A lightweight unit of execution within a process that shares memory with other threads
A CPU core
An independent program with its own memory

exercises.question: How do threads in the same process share data?
exercises.answer: They directly access the shared heap and global variables
exercises.explain: Threads within one process share address space. They can read and write the same memory without system calls. This is fast but requires synchronization.
choices: They directly access the shared heap and global variables
Through message passing only
Through operating system mechanisms like sockets
They cannot share data directly

exercises.question: What is the main advantage of threads over processes?
exercises.answer: Threads are lightweight and cheap to create; data sharing is fast
exercises.explain: Creating a thread is much faster than creating a process. Threads can share data via memory without IPC overhead. Threads in one process are cheaper to manage.
choices: Threads cannot crash the program
Threads are more secure
Threads are lightweight and cheap to create; data sharing is fast
Threads run on multiple cores automatically

exercises.question: When one thread crashes, what happens to other threads in the same process?
exercises.answer: The entire process usually terminates
exercises.explain: If one thread crashes (undefined behavior, segfault), it damages the process's shared memory. The OS usually kills the whole process to prevent data corruption.
choices: Other threads are temporarily paused then resume
The OS automatically isolates the crashed thread
The entire process usually terminates
Other threads continue unaffected

exercises.question: Which is true about thread stacks?
exercises.answer: Each thread has its own stack but shares the heap
exercises.explain: Threads have separate stacks so local variables and return addresses are independent. But they share the heap, global variables, and file descriptors.
choices: Each thread has its own stack but shares the heap
All threads share one stack
Each thread has its own heap
Stacks are not used in threaded programs

units.title: Race Conditions and Critical Sections
units.tip: A race condition occurs when the result of a concurrent program depends on the timing of thread execution. A critical section is a code segment that accesses shared data and must run without interference from other threads.

exercises.question: What is a race condition?
exercises.answer: The outcome depends on the relative timing of concurrent thread operations
exercises.explain: A race condition occurs when the result of a program is unpredictable because different thread orderings produce different results. The outcome races between threads.
choices: Two threads trying to access the same file
A thread accessing memory that was deleted
A thread waiting too long for another
The outcome depends on the relative timing of concurrent thread operations

exercises.question: Consider two threads incrementing a shared counter. Without synchronization, what can go wrong?
exercises.answer: Lost updates: both threads may read the old value, increment it, and write the same result
exercises.explain: Increment is not atomic. Thread A reads 5, Thread B reads 5, both increment, both write 6. The final result is 6 instead of 7. Updates are lost.
choices: The counter becomes negative
Only one thread can increment at a time
The counter crashes
Lost updates: both threads may read the old value, increment it, and write the same result

exercises.question: Why is x++ not thread-safe?
exercises.answer: It is three operations (read, increment, write) that can interleave between threads
exercises.explain: x++ expands to: temp = x; temp++; x = temp. Threads can interleave, causing lost updates.
choices: The compiler removes it
It only works with integers
It is three operations (read, increment, write) that can interleave between threads
The CPU does not understand ++

exercises.question: What does it mean if a race condition is hard to reproduce?
exercises.answer: It occurs only with specific thread timing combinations that are rare
exercises.explain: Race conditions often appear sporadically. They depend on CPU scheduling, cache behavior, and thread timing, which vary. A crash might occur once in a million runs.
choices: It only happens on multi-core systems
The bug is in the testing code
The race condition does not really exist
It occurs only with specific thread timing combinations that are rare

exercises.question: How can race conditions cause data corruption?
exercises.answer: Threads read partially-written data or overwrite each other's writes
exercises.explain: If Thread A is writing a struct and Thread B reads it mid-write, B sees garbage. Or Thread A overwrites what Thread B just wrote, losing B's update.
choices: The operating system always prevents it
Only by directly deleting the data
Race conditions only affect speed, not correctness
Threads read partially-written data or overwrite each other's writes

exercises.question: What is a critical section?
exercises.answer: Code that accesses shared data and must run without interference from other threads
exercises.explain: A critical section is a region where only one thread should execute at a time. Entering a critical section without permission from other threads causes races.
choices: Code that accesses shared data and must run without interference from other threads
A thread priority setting
An error handling section
The main function of a program

exercises.question: What is mutual exclusion (mutex)?
exercises.answer: Ensuring only one thread enters a critical section at a time
exercises.explain: Mutual exclusion means mutually excluding other threads. Only one thread can be in the critical section; others wait outside.
choices: Ensuring only one thread enters a critical section at a time
Preventing all threads from running
Eliminating shared data
Allowing multiple threads to run in parallel

exercises.question: Which line is the critical section in: print('start'); shared.count++; print('done');
exercises.answer: shared.count++
exercises.explain: Only shared.count++ touches shared data, so only it needs protection. The print lines use no shared state.
choices: print('done')
print('start')
shared.count++
All three lines equally

exercises.question: What is the goal of critical section protection?
exercises.answer: Maintain consistency of shared data and prevent unpredictable interleaving
exercises.explain: Protected critical sections guarantee that operations complete atomically. Shared data stays consistent. Results are predictable regardless of thread timing.
choices: To eliminate multithreading
To make the program run faster
To reduce memory usage
Maintain consistency of shared data and prevent unpredictable interleaving

exercises.question: Why not just protect everything with locks?
exercises.answer: Locking too much reduces parallelism and performance; only critical sections need protection
exercises.explain: Excessive locking serializes the program and defeats concurrency benefits. Only code that accesses shared data needs protection. Other code runs in parallel.
choices: Locking too much reduces parallelism and performance; only critical sections need protection
Locks are slow and always cause deadlocks
All code must be protected equally
Locks do not actually protect anything

units.title: Locks and Mutexes
units.tip: A lock is a synchronization primitive that protects critical sections. A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) is the simplest lock type. A thread acquires a lock before entering a critical section and releases it when done.

exercises.question: How does a mutex work?
exercises.answer: Only one thread can hold the mutex at a time; others wait
exercises.explain: A mutex is a binary lock. A thread acquires it before entering a critical section. Other threads block waiting for it. The owner releases it when done.
choices: Only one thread can hold the mutex at a time; others wait
All threads can hold it simultaneously
It automatically fixes race conditions
It prevents threads from running

exercises.question: What does lock() do?
exercises.answer: Acquires the mutex; waits if another thread holds it
exercises.explain: lock() is a blocking call. If the mutex is free, it acquires it immediately. If held by another thread, the caller blocks until released.
choices: Destroys the mutex
Releases the mutex immediately
Acquires the mutex; waits if another thread holds it
Checks if the mutex is locked without blocking

exercises.question: What does unlock() do?
exercises.answer: Releases the mutex so other waiting threads can acquire it
exercises.explain: unlock() releases ownership. If threads are waiting, the OS scheduler picks one to wake up and acquire the mutex.
choices: Destroys the mutex
Releases the mutex so other waiting threads can acquire it
Locks the mutex again
Wakes all threads

exercises.question: Why must you always unlock a mutex you locked?
exercises.answer: Otherwise other threads wait forever (deadlock); the program hangs
exercises.explain: Forgetting unlock() is a critical bug. The mutex remains held. Threads waiting for it block indefinitely. The program appears hung.
choices: Unlocking is optional
It wastes CPU
The mutex automatically unlocks after a timeout
Otherwise other threads wait forever (deadlock); the program hangs

exercises.question: What is a common pattern for using mutexes?
exercises.answer: lock(); try { ... } finally { unlock(); }
exercises.explain: This ensures unlock() runs even if an exception occurs. Some languages use RAII or defer to automate this.
choices: Unlock before locking
Never unlock, just create a new mutex
lock(); try { ... } finally { unlock(); }
lock(); ... unlock(); at different times

exercises.question: What is a reentrant lock?
exercises.answer: A lock that the same thread can acquire multiple times
exercises.explain: A reentrant (recursive) lock allows one thread to lock it multiple times. It has a counter. Each lock increments; each unlock decrements.
choices: A lock that the same thread can acquire multiple times
A lock shared by all processes
A lock that prevents threads from entering
A lock that cannot be used

exercises.question: What typically happens if a non-reentrant mutex is locked twice by the same thread?
exercises.answer: Deadlock: the thread waits for itself forever
exercises.explain: The thread already holds the mutex. Trying to lock it again blocks the thread on a lock it owns. This typically deadlocks, though some mutexes report an error instead.
choices: The second lock is granted immediately
The mutex disappears
Deadlock: the thread waits for itself forever
The thread is woken up automatically

exercises.question: What is lock contention?
exercises.answer: Multiple threads competing for the same lock, causing waiting and reduced parallelism
exercises.explain: High contention means many threads want the same lock. Most block waiting. Throughput drops because threads serialize. Low contention means fast lock acquisition.
choices: A thread that never releases a lock
A type of deadlock
Multiple threads competing for the same lock, causing waiting and reduced parallelism
A lock that is poorly designed

exercises.question: How can you reduce lock contention?
exercises.answer: Use fine-grained locks, protect smaller critical sections, minimize time holding locks
exercises.explain: Instead of one big lock, use multiple locks for different data. Keep critical sections short. Release locks as soon as possible. This lets threads run in parallel longer.
choices: Use a global lock for all data
Use fine-grained locks, protect smaller critical sections, minimize time holding locks
Increase the number of threads
Never use locks

exercises.question: What is a spinlock?
exercises.answer: A lock that makes waiting threads spin in a loop instead of blocking
exercises.explain: A spinlock is a busy-wait mechanism. The waiting thread loops checking the lock instead of sleeping. Spinlocks waste CPU but have low latency for short waits.
choices: A type of condition variable
A lock that makes waiting threads spin in a loop instead of blocking
A rotating mechanical lock
A lock for threads

units.title: Deadlock and Synchronization
units.tip: Deadlock occurs when threads wait for each other in a cycle and none can proceed. Atomic operations ensure an operation completes without interruption. Synchronization primitives like semaphores coordinate multiple threads.

exercises.question: What is deadlock?
exercises.answer: Threads waiting for each other in a cycle, unable to proceed
exercises.explain: Deadlock is a permanent block. Thread A holds lock X and waits for Y. Thread B holds Y and waits for X. Neither can proceed. The program hangs.
choices: Threads waiting for each other in a cycle, unable to proceed
A memory error
Multiple threads running
A slow CPU

exercises.question: What are the four conditions necessary for deadlock?
exercises.answer: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait
exercises.explain: Mutual exclusion: locks are exclusive. Hold and wait: threads hold locks while waiting for others. No preemption: locks cannot be forcibly taken. Circular wait: a cycle of waiting.
choices: Input, output, processing, storage
Threads, memory, CPU, time
Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait
Locks, files, messages, events

exercises.question: How can you prevent deadlock by imposing lock ordering?
exercises.answer: All threads acquire locks in the same order, breaking circular wait
exercises.explain: If all threads acquire lock A before lock B, a cycle cannot form. Thread holding A waits for B (not B for A). This breaks the circular wait condition.
choices: Never use locks together
Use only one lock
All threads acquire locks in the same order, breaking circular wait
Increase thread priority

exercises.question: What is a classic example of deadlock?
exercises.answer: Two people, two chopsticks, each needs both to eat (Dining Philosophers)
exercises.explain: Each philosopher picks up one chopstick then waits for the other. If all pick left first, no one gets right. All wait forever.
choices: Too many threads
Two people, two chopsticks, each needs both to eat (Dining Philosophers)
A thread reading a variable twice
Two threads sharing one variable

exercises.question: How can you detect if your program is deadlocked?
exercises.answer: The program hangs and does not respond; threads are waiting on locks
exercises.explain: Deadlock shows as the program freezing. Debugging tools show all threads blocked waiting for locks, often in a cycle. No thread is making progress.
choices: The program crashes immediately
The program uses too much memory
The program hangs and does not respond; threads are waiting on locks
The program is too fast

exercises.question: What is an atomic operation?
exercises.answer: An operation that completes entirely without interruption by other threads
exercises.explain: Atomic means indivisible. An atomic operation either happens fully or not at all. Other threads cannot observe a partial state.
choices: An operation that completes entirely without interruption by other threads
An operation on an atom data type
A slow operation
An operation using atoms

exercises.question: What is an atomic variable?
exercises.answer: A variable whose read and write operations are guaranteed atomic
exercises.explain: Languages like Java and C++ offer atomic variables. Load, store, and compare-and-swap operations are atomic without explicit locks.
choices: A variable in a separate thread
A variable that cannot change
A variable that loses updates
A variable whose read and write operations are guaranteed atomic

exercises.question: What is a semaphore?
exercises.answer: A synchronization primitive with a counter; threads wait until the counter is positive
exercises.explain: A semaphore is an integer with two operations: wait() (decrement, block if 0) and signal() (increment, wake waiting threads). Used for resource counting.
choices: A synchronization primitive with a counter; threads wait until the counter is positive
A traffic signal
A type of mutex
A memory error detector

exercises.question: How does a binary semaphore differ from a regular semaphore?
exercises.answer: A binary semaphore is 0 or 1 only; a regular semaphore can be any non-negative integer
exercises.explain: A binary semaphore acts like a mutex (two states). A regular semaphore counts resources, allowing N threads to enter if initialized to N.
choices: They are the same thing
Binary semaphores are faster
A binary semaphore is 0 or 1 only; a regular semaphore can be any non-negative integer
Binary semaphores are unsafe

exercises.question: How can a semaphore control access to a pool of N resources?
exercises.answer: Initialize the semaphore to N; each thread wait() on it before using a resource
exercises.explain: If there are 5 printers, create a semaphore initialized to 5. Each thread wait() (acquire) before printing, signal() (release) after. At most 5 print concurrently.
choices: Use a mutex for each resource
Semaphores cannot control pools
Initialize the semaphore to N; each thread wait() on it before using a resource
Use one semaphore per resource

units.title: Advanced Concurrency
units.tip: Async/await simplifies concurrent code by allowing functions to pause and resume. Event loops schedule tasks without explicit thread management. Message passing avoids shared mutable state.

exercises.question: What is async/await?
exercises.answer: Language syntax allowing functions to pause waiting for I/O and resume later
exercises.explain: async/await lets you write concurrent code that looks sequential. The function pauses at an await point, letting other code run. When I/O completes, it resumes.
choices: A type of mutex
A loop construct
A way to make threads faster
Language syntax allowing functions to pause waiting for I/O and resume later

exercises.question: What is an event loop?
exercises.answer: A scheduler that runs tasks and I/O callbacks, processing one at a time
exercises.explain: An event loop sits in a loop waiting for events (I/O completion, timers, signals). When an event fires, it calls the registered handler. No explicit threads needed.
choices: A scheduler that runs tasks and I/O callbacks, processing one at a time
A loop in your code
A type of deadlock
A thread that runs continuously

exercises.question: How does an event loop enable concurrency without threads?
exercises.answer: Tasks yield while waiting for I/O; the loop runs other tasks instead of blocking
exercises.explain: When a task awaits I/O, it yields control. The event loop runs other tasks. When I/O completes, the event loop resumes the first task. No extra threads are needed.
choices: Tasks yield while waiting for I/O; the loop runs other tasks instead of blocking
It uses multiple CPUs
It eliminates I/O altogether
Threads are hidden inside

exercises.question: What happens if you call a blocking function inside an async task?
exercises.answer: It blocks the entire event loop; other tasks cannot run
exercises.explain: Blocking calls pause the whole event loop. If a task does a synchronous file read, no other task runs until it completes. This defeats the purpose of async.
choices: It blocks the entire event loop; other tasks cannot run
Only that task blocks
The event loop automatically handles it
The event loop ignores it

exercises.question: What languages commonly use async/await?
exercises.answer: JavaScript, Python, C#, Rust, and others
exercises.explain: Async/await is a widely adopted pattern. C# introduced it, and JavaScript, Python, Rust, and Kotlin adopted it. It simplifies concurrent I/O operations.
choices: No languages support it
Only Python
Only Java
JavaScript, Python, C#, Rust, and others

exercises.question: What is message passing?
exercises.answer: Threads communicate by sending messages through channels instead of sharing memory
exercises.explain: Message passing avoids shared mutable state. One thread sends a message to another. The receiver reads the message. No locks or race conditions on the message itself.
choices: Threads reading each other's memory
A type of mutex
Threads communicate by sending messages through channels instead of sharing memory
Email between computers

exercises.question: What is a channel?
exercises.answer: A queue connecting two or more threads for message passing
exercises.explain: A channel is a bounded or unbounded queue. One end is a sender, the other a receiver. Sending adds a message; receiving removes it.
choices: A network port
A queue connecting two or more threads for message passing
A type of mutex
A communication protocol

exercises.question: Why is message passing safer than shared memory?
exercises.answer: No race conditions on message contents; ownership transfers from sender to receiver
exercises.explain: The sender and receiver do not both access the same message. Ownership is explicit. Languages like Rust enforce this at compile time.
choices: It is slower so bugs hide
It uses more memory
No race conditions on message contents; ownership transfers from sender to receiver
Channels cannot fail

exercises.question: What happens if a receiver waits on an empty channel and a sender is still alive but never sends?
exercises.answer: The receiver blocks indefinitely
exercises.explain: With no message arriving and a sender still open, the receiver waits forever. If all senders are closed, most channel designs report that instead of blocking.
choices: The receiver blocks indefinitely
The program crashes
The receiver unblocks immediately
The receiver gets a default value

exercises.question: How does Rust enforce safety in message passing?
exercises.answer: Sending a value moves ownership, so the sender can no longer use it
exercises.explain: Rust's ownership system moves a value into the channel. The compiler then rejects any later use by the sender, so two threads never access it at once.
choices: Rust does not enforce safety
Sending a value moves ownership, so the sender can no longer use it
Using runtime checks only
Rust uses message passing instead of channels
